`SimNet` provides tools to simulate stochastic disease transmission through
temporal contact networks and to infer the contact structure most likely to
explain observed infection events.

This vignette presents a simple workflow using **simulated data only**. We
create a population, generate alternative temporal contact networks, simulate
transmission through one known network, and then use the simulated infection
history to infer the causative transmission network.

The example is intentionally smaller than the simulations used in the
manuscript so that it can be run quickly.

</p>

4. [Simulate disease transmission](#st)  
   4.1. [Infection-status matrix](#status)

## Install and load SimNet {#ip}

The latest development version of `SimNet` can be installed from GitHub:

```{r installation, eval=FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("Hector-Marina/SimNet", build_vignettes=TRUE)
```

Load the package before starting the simulation:

```{r load-package, eval=FALSE}
library(SimNet)
```

## Create a simulated population {#sp}

A simulation starts by creating a `simPOP` object with `simplePOP()`. The
object stores the individuals, simulation steps, replicates, contact networks,
infection histories, and transmission information generated during the
workflow. We simulate 200 individuals (`NIDs`) over 100 time steps (`steps`) and 100
replicates (`rep`):

```{r create-population}
set.seed(123)
POP=simplePOP(NIDs=200,steps=100,rep=100)
POP
```


## Simulate temporal contact networks {#scn}

Transmission may be compatible with several contact structures recorded over
the same period. We therefore generate alternative temporal contact networks
that will later be evaluated as candidate transmission pathways.

The example contains five networks:

- `SIN`: **S**ocial **I**nteraction **N**etwork;
- `ASN`: **A**rea **S**imilarity **N**etwork;
- `MPN`: Object-mediated **M**ilking **P**arlour **N**etwork;
- `RCN`: Object-mediated **R**esting **C**ubicle **N**etwork; and
- `NCN`: **N**aïve homogeneous-mixing **C**ontact **N**etwork.

### Direct contact networks {#direct}

`simCONT()` generates weighted temporal networks with gamma-distributed edge
weights and temporal correlation between consecutive steps.

Here, two independent networks are generated to represent two alternative
spatially derived contact networks following [Marina et al., (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1016/J.APPLANIM.2024.106366)

```{r direct-networks}
POP=simCONT(POP=POP, NameCont="SIN", gshape=1, gscale=5, val=1, rho=0.25, verbose=FALSE)
POP=simCONT(POP=POP, NameCont="ASN", gshape=1, gscale=5, val=1, rho=0.25, verbose=FALSE)
```


### Object-mediated contact networks {#object}

`simOBJ()` generates directed networks based on the sequential use of shared
objects. An individual can therefore transmit only to individuals using the
same object later in the sequence. We simulate two object-mediated contact 
structures:

```{r object-networks}
POP=simOBJ(POP=POP, NameCont="MPN", pos=24,  freq=2, val=12, verbose=FALSE)
POP=simOBJ(POP=POP, NameCont="RCN", pos=200, freq=5, val=4,  verbose=FALSE)
```

### Naive contact network {#naive}

Finally, `uniCONT()` creates a Naïve homogeneous-mixing contact network in which 
every individual is connected to every other individual with the same edge weight.
This provides a naïve reference scenario without restrictions imposed by a
specific contact structure.

```{r naive-network}
POP=uniCONT(POP=POP, NameCont="NCN", val=1, verbose=FALSE)
POP
```

The `simPOP` object now contains all candidate temporal contact networks used
in the following transmission simulation and inference.


## Simulate disease transmission {#st}

We next simulate transmission through one of the candidate networks using
`SIRmod()`. Because the true transmission network is known in a simulation,
the result can later be used to evaluate whether the inference procedure
recovers the correct network. The `beta` and `gamma` values, and the number of 
initially infected individuals have been derived from [Woudstra et al., (2023)](https://doi.org/10.3168/jds.2022-22942)

```{r simulate-transmission}
beta=0.000172244
gamma=0.0358299
NID_inf=sample(1:100,7)
```


In this example, transmission is simulated through the **SIN** using an SIS
model. Seven individuals are infectious at the first time step.

```{r simulate-transmission-tva}
POP=SIRmod(POP=POP, NameCont="MPN", beta=beta, gamma=gamma, epsilon=NULL,
           IDseed=NID_inf, verbose=FALSE)
POP
```

Successful transmission events are stored in `POP@TransDF`:

```{r transmission-events}
head(POP@TransDF)
```


### Infection-status matrix {#status}

The infection history of one replicate can be visualised as a status matrix:

```{r plot-status}
plot(POP, rep=1, type="inf.mat")
```


### Infection dynamics {#dynamics}

The temporal dynamics across all replicates can also be visualised directly
from the `simPOP` object:

```{r plot-dynamics}
plot(POP, type="inf.curv")
```


## Infer the causative transmission network {#itp}

The infection status generated above is now treated as the observed infection
history. All five contact networks are evaluated as alternative explanations
for the transmission events.

Although we know that the SIN generated the infections, this information is
not supplied to the inference procedure.

### Estimate transmission probabilities {#riskcont}

`RISKcont()` estimates, for every newly infected individual, the probability
that the infection could have occurred through each candidate contact network.
The Homogeneus-mixing contact network, a.k.a. NCN, is used as the reference network:

```{r infer-network}
POP=RISKcont(POP=POP, NameCont=names(POP@ContactM), ref="NCN", verbose=FALSE)
```

A transmission probability of zero indicates that an infection event was
incompatible with that contact network because no infectious individual could
explain the observed infection through the corresponding contacts.

The proportion of impossible events can be summarised as:

```{r impossible-events}
round(tapply(POP@RISKcont$TProb,POP@RISKcont$ContactM,
             function(x) mean(x==0, na.rm=TRUE)),3)
```


### Compare candidate networks {#compare}

Event-level probabilities can be combined within replicate to calculate the
likelihood associated with each candidate contact network:

```{r network-likelihood}
L=aggregate(TProb ~ Replicate + ContactM, data=POP@RISKcont,FUN=prod)
Lmean=tapply( L$TProb,  L$ContactM,  mean, na.rm=TRUE)
round(Lmean/Lmean["NCN"],2)
```

Values above `1` indicate greater support than the reference network (NCN).

The relative transmission probabilities can be visualised using
`plotRISKcont2()`. The figure is printed directly in the vignette and is not
saved to an external file.

```{r plot-network-inference}
plotRISKcont2(POP, ref="NCN", Nsim="MPN-simulated Transmission")
```


## Final remarks {#final}

This example illustrates the basic `SimNet` simulation-to-inference workflow:

```text
simPOP
  -> temporal contact networks
  -> stochastic transmission
  -> observed infection history
  -> candidate-network probabilities
  -> inferred transmission network
```

Because the example uses simulated data, the true causative network is known
and the inference results can be compared directly with the network used to
generate transmission.

Larger populations, longer simulation periods, additional replicates, and
alternative transmission scenarios can be explored using the same workflow.

We hope that `SimNet` provides a useful and flexible framework for exploring 
plausible transmission routes for different infectious pathogens.

For further details on individual functions and their available arguments, 
please refer to the corresponding help pages using `?function_name`.

Thank you for using `SimNet` — and happy transmission tracking! 🐄🦠🧫
